gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Avantree PowerByte's 20-hour claim rests on a 26.6 Wh pack (7.4 V × 3,600 mAh), which works out to an average draw of about 1.3 W at the manual's stated 50% volume. That is about 4% of the 30 W rating, and at the full rated 30 W the pack could not last even 1 hour.
standout_why: I opened two rival pages. itechguides 'Best Bluetooth Speakers with FM Radio: 3 Top Picks for 2026' gives mAh for only two products, gives no cell voltage, and computes no Wh, average draw or cost per Wh. powersof10 'Best Bluetooth Speakers with Radio 2026' gives mAh for three products but never converts to Wh. It reports its own hour counts for other speakers, not the PowerByte, lists the SP850 only as 3 W, and gives two different numbers for how much less battery radio mode uses (40% and 30–40%). Neither page puts a pack's energy next to its wattage rating. I did not open the geekchamp, rottenwifi, sekin, gagadget or mobilestalk pages, so the score stays at 2 rather than 3.
decides: It changes how the pick should be stated. ChatGPT made the PowerByte its 'Best for powerful sound' card and listed 20 hours and 30 W together, but the pack can't deliver both at once. The 20 hours only holds at about 1.3 W average (50% volume), and a 26.6 Wh pack driven at the full 30 W rating would be flat in under 0.9 h. The PowerByte still has the most stored energy of the candidates I could source: 26.6 Wh against 3.7 Wh for the SP850, about 7.2 times as much. That makes it the right pick for long radio listening at moderate volume, at $3.75 per Wh against $10.00 per Wh for the SP850. It is the wrong pick for loud listening for a whole afternoon on battery.
